notes.meaning: Nehemiah the governor and a leader named Zedekiah put their seals on the written covenant. A seal was a stamped mark of wax or clay that officially signed an agreement. Nehemiah signed first because of his high rank as governor, setting a faithful example for the entire nation. Leaders honor God when they are the first to commit to his ways.

These verses list the priests who signed the document on behalf of their priestly families. Men like Seraiah, Jeremiah, and Amariah stood as representatives for their relatives. Since every person in the land could not affix a personal seal, these leaders acted for their family lines.

The list of priestly family heads continues with Harim, Daniel, Meshullam, and several others. These men affirmed the solemn covenant, stepping forward to lead the worshiping community back to God's ways. Good spiritual leaders show the way by committing themselves first.

Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah complete the list of the twenty-one priests who sealed the document. These men represented the divisions of priests serving at the altar. By putting their names to the agreement, they pledged that the priests would honor God's law in the temple.

Next, the Levites sealed the covenant, beginning with Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, and their fellow ministers. Levites were temple assistants from the tribe of Levi who helped the priests and taught the people. Several of these men had just led the congregation in reading the law and offering the great prayer of confession.

The list of Levites finishes with Zaccur, Sherebiah, Bani, and their brothers, bringing the total to seventeen Levite leaders. They had urged the people to turn back to God, and now they placed their own seals on the promise. Leaders must always be willing to practice what they teach.

The leaders of the common people signed next, starting with well-known family names such as Parosh, Pahath-moab, and Elam. Many of these family names match the clans that first returned from exile in Babylon years earlier. These civil leaders used their public influence to guide their families toward obeying God.

The roster of family heads continues with Ater, Hezekiah, Azzur, Hodiah, Hashum, and others. Each family head represented a large group of relatives and local towns. Their participation showed that the renewal of faith reached into every corner of ordinary life.

More family leaders follow, including Magpiash, Meshullam, Zadok, and Pelatiah. These respected elders openly stood up for God's truth before the whole congregation. Their agreement united the community behind the sacred promise.

Hoshea, Hallohesh, Rehum, and other clan leaders added their seals to the document. In all, forty-four leaders of the people signed the covenant alongside the priests and Levites. They took personal responsibility for keeping the nation faithful to the Lord.

The list of community leaders concludes with Ahijah, Hanan, Anan, Malluch, Harim, and Baanah. With eighty-four leaders having sealed the document, the formal signing was complete. These men pledged their honor and their authority to uphold God's law.

The rest of the community—including temple singers, gatekeepers, and servants—readily agreed to the covenant. This included foreign converts who had left pagan practices to follow God, along with wives and children old enough to understand. Everyone who was capable of knowing right from wrong took part in this commitment.

The people joined their leaders by making a solemn vow to obey all the laws God gave through Moses. They entered into an oath and a curse, asking God to punish them if they willfully broke their word. High and low stood together as brothers, pledging wholehearted obedience to the Lord.

The first specific promise was that the people would not intermarry with the surrounding pagan nations. In those days, parents arranged marriages, so this command directly addressed the fathers and mothers. They agreed to keep their families separate from idol worship so their faith would remain pure.

The people promised to keep the Sabbath and sacred feast days holy by refusing to buy goods or food from foreign traders. They also promised to let their farmland rest every seventh year and to forgive debts owed by fellow Israelites. Obeying God's calendar showed that they trusted him to provide for their needs rather than relying on unfair profit.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that this verse combines rules from different parts of the Pentateuch, showing that the post-exilic community possessed and honored the complete books of Moses.

notes.meaning: The Israelites placed a voluntary yearly tax of one-third of a shekel on every person to fund the temple services. The law of Moses had required a half-shekel, but the amount was likely lowered here because the returning community was so poor. Even in hard times, they made sure to support public worship together.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that a third of a Persian shekel equaled the silver weight of the older Hebrew half-shekel, or that the Exodus rule was a census tax rather than an annual fee.

notes.meaning: This money paid for the bread placed on the golden table, the daily burnt offerings, and the special sacrifices for Sabbaths and festivals. It also supplied the sin offerings that made atonement—covering the people's sins to restore their peace with God. Public worship required steady supplies, so everyone shared the cost.

The priests, Levites, and people cast lots to decide which family would bring firewood to the altar at each time of year. God's law required the altar fire to burn continually, which required a vast and steady supply of wood. Casting lots ensured that every family took an orderly, fair turn in serving God's house.

The people promised to bring the first portion of their crops and fruit trees to the house of the Lord each year. Giving these firstfruits was an act of faith, thanking God before the rest of the harvest was even gathered. Believers show gratitude by giving God their first and best.

They also promised to present their firstborn sons and livestock to the priests, just as Moses had commanded. Firstborn sons and unclean animals were redeemed by paying a set redemption price to the priests, while clean animals were offered as sacrifices. This reminded the people that every life belongs to God.

The people pledged to bring the first portions of their dough, fruit, wine, and oil to the temple storerooms for the priests. They also agreed to give a tithe—a tenth of their farm produce—to the Levites in every farming town. These gifts provided the daily food the ministers needed so they could focus on serving the Lord.

differ.view: Giving a tenth of one's income remains a binding command for Christians today to support the work of the church.
Tithing was part of the Old Testament law for Israel, so Christians are called to give generously and cheerfully without a required percentage.

notes.meaning: An Aaronite priest was to go with the Levites when they collected the tithes in the countryside. Then the Levites were to bring a tenth of that collection—the tithe of the tithes—to the temple treasury for the priests. Having a priest present ensured honesty and prevented anyone from cheating.

The Israelites and Levites were to deliver these offerings to the temple storerooms, where the sacred vessels were kept and where the ministers stayed. The people concluded their covenant with a clear vow: they would never neglect or abandon God's house. When God's people honor his worship, their spiritual life stays strong.
